title: Indian Railways Pantry Staff Cook Oats for Toddler on Long Journey
excerpt: A mother on a Bihar-to-Bengaluru trip asked the pantry car to prepare the oats she had packed for her 2-year-old — staff had it ready in five minutes, and her Instagram post is winning hearts.
body:
• A mother travelling from Bihar to Bengaluru with her 2-year-old son asked the train's pantry staff to cook a packet of oats she had packed — and they had it back to her in about five minutes.
  • "They were so cooperative and welcoming, and there was absolutely no hesitation in helping a mother travelling with her baby," she wrote on Instagram.
  • Travelling with a baby by train? Her formula works: pack shelf-stable food in packets (oats, cereal, formula) plus a small container, and ask the pantry car staff in the evening — they did the cooking in minutes.
  • Her post, shared by Instagram user @dakshnmom, drew warm responses, with other parents adding their own stories of help from railway pantry crews.

Five minutes of kindness

Travelling with a toddler on a two-night train journey tests even the best-prepared parent. For Instagram user @dakshnmom, travelling from Bihar to Bengaluru with her 2-year-old son, one small gesture changed the entire trip.

She had planned ahead: a packet of oats and a small container, packed from home so she would not have to rely entirely on outside food for her child's dinner. In the evening, she walked to the pantry car and asked the staff if they could prepare the oats for her toddler. She was not expecting much.

"They took my oats packet, prepared it for me, and within just five minutes, they handed it back to me, freshly made and ready for my little one," she wrote in the Instagram post shared by India Today and Curly Tales.

"Sometimes, it's these little gestures that make a long journey so much easier and memorable. A little kindness along the way makes a BIG difference."

— @dakshnmom, on Instagram

Context & background

Feeding young children on Indian trains is one of the quiet stresses of family travel. Pantry car food is designed for adult passengers, and many parents of toddlers — wary of spice levels, hygiene, or simply a child's picky habits — prefer to carry their own supplies. That usually means dry cereal, formula, or oats, all of which need hot water or a stove to become dinner.

What stood out here was not just the cooking but the attitude. "They were so cooperative and welcoming, and there was absolutely no hesitation in helping a mother travelling with her baby," the mother wrote — a line that resonated because pantry staff, working a packed kitchen through long hauls, are rarely asked for custom favours and often decline them.

Impact & analysis

The post struck a chord precisely because it counters the default narrative around Indian Railways' food service. Public conversation tends to run on complaints — hygiene lapses, overpricing, quality — and genuine problems do exist. But the flood of responses, with other parents sharing their own stories of pantry staff going out of their way for young children, suggests a quieter, warmer layer of the railway experience that rarely makes headlines.

There is a practical lesson in it too. The mother's approach worked because she did the prep herself: she brought the dry ingredients and the container, made a polite request, and asked at a manageable hour of the evening rather than at the dinner rush. Staff with a working pantry kitchen can do the rest in minutes. For parents, that is a repeatable playbook — and it beats arriving at the station dependent on whatever the platform vendors happen to sell.

Diaspora angle

For diaspora families visiting India, long-distance train travel is often part of the trip — the overnight journey that becomes a childhood memory. This story is a small reminder of the warmth that still defines much of Indian public life, and a useful tip: if you are doing the Grand Trunk Express with a toddler, pack the oats and the tiffin box, and ask the pantry crew. They may surprise you.

What's next

Indian Railways has spent years modernising catering — e-catering apps, branded food plazas, base kitchens with CCTV monitoring. But no app replicates what happened here. The next frontier for passenger comfort may not be technology at all: it could be as simple as making "we'll cook what you packed" an informal norm for travelling parents.
